topic: Decoding Epidemics: The SIR Model Mechanics

outline.topic: Decoding Epidemics: The SIR Model Mechanics

sections.title: Introduction: Why Do Outbreaks Spread?
sections.content: Briefly introduce the concept of infectious disease spread. Define the three key compartments: Susceptible (S), Infectious (I), and Recovered (R). Emphasize that individuals transition between these states.
sections.example: Visualize a group of healthy students in a classroom where one person enters with a cold.

sections.title: Defining the Compartments and Dynamics
sections.content: Explain the mechanics: S to I (infection rate β) and I to R (recovery rate γ). Use a flow diagram with directional arrows to show the 'one-way' transition of population segments.
sections.example: A 'health bar' animation: S (Green) turns into I (Red) upon contact, and I (Red) turns into R (Blue) after a set time.

sections.title: The Core Equations: The Math of Flow
sections.content: Introduce the differential equations (dS/dt, dI/dt, dR/dt). Use graphical representation: show how the slope of the 'I' curve is determined by the intersection of the new infection rate and the recovery rate.
sections.example: A water tank analogy: Water flowing from Tank S to Tank I depends on the faucet width (β), and Tank I to Tank R depends on the drain width (γ).

sections.title: Critical Thresholds: The R₀ Concept
sections.content: Explain the Basic Reproduction Number (R₀). Define it as the ratio of β/γ. Explain that if R₀ > 1, the infection propagates; if R₀ < 1, it dies out.
sections.example: An animation showing a virus spreading to 3 neighbors vs. 0.5 neighbors, illustrating the 'tipping point'.

sections.title: Simulation & Application: Flattening the Curve
sections.content: Demonstrate how changing parameters (like social distancing to reduce β) changes the shape of the 'I' curve on a graph. Summarize the model's predictive power for public health.
sections.example: A simulation showing a 'spiky' graph (no intervention) vs. a 'flat' graph (simulating masks/quarantine), saving hospital capacity.

storyboard.title: Introduction: Why Do Outbreaks Spread?
lecture_lines: People fall into three health states.
Susceptible: healthy, yet to be exposed.
Infected: currently carrying and spreading disease.
Recovered: immune or no longer infectious.

storyboard.title: Defining the Compartments and Dynamics
lecture_lines: Susceptible individuals become infected by contact.
Infected individuals eventually transition to recovered.

storyboard.title: The Core Equations: The Math of Flow
lecture_lines: Math models describe these flow rates.
Rates depend on contact and recovery.
The equations map population state changes.

storyboard.title: Critical Thresholds: The R₀ Concept
lecture_lines: R-naught over one means epidemic growth.

storyboard.title: Simulation & Application: Flattening the Curve
lecture_lines: Lowering contact flattens the infection curve.
Models help manage health system capacity.
